newsitem.title: USA: IMF, World Bank face new realities at annual meet.
newsitem.headline: IMF, World Bank face new realities at annual meet.

text.p: With the global financial system in a period of unprecedented change, the role of the International Monetary Fund and World Bank seem both enhanced, yet somehow diminished.
Only a handful of countries still shun membership in the two lending institutions, so they are able to carry their message and their assistance far and wide as never before.

At the same time, the multi-trillion dollar private markets are holding such sway these days -- effortlessly moving money across borders into emerging economies -- that they make the power of the IMF and Bank appear less relevant.

"The world of foreign financial involvement in developing economies and emerging markets is being driven today by private capital, by private investors, by private lenders," said Charles Dallara, managing director of the Institute of International Finance.

"I think there is a very different set of rules for the IMF and World Bank today. They no longer are the dominant supplier of finance -- in fact on a net basis in the aggregate they provide very little in finance for these countries," Dallara adds.

It is against this backdrop that the two institutions begin their annual meetings this week, as they attempt to deal with issues ranging from a controversial new debt relief initiative to ways to head off global economic crisis.
Much of the discussion reflects the disturbing ability of the tightly-woven international financial system to quickly spread problems from one country to others around the world.

This was most recently seen during what IMF Managing Director Michel Camdessus has called the first economic crisis of the 21st century, the unraveling of Mexico that required a Herculean international rescue effort to repair its economy.

That experience helped spawned several initiatives, including a new IMF bulletin board on the Internet on which users can be directed to country data in a number of emerging markets on a more timely basis.

This seemed key since the 1994-1995 Mexican peso crisis caught many investors off guard and spread quickly to some of its surrounding neighbors and even countries in Eastern Europe. Critics said the crisis might have been avoided if data on the Mexican economy was more readily available.

"The new IMF standards will improve the availability, the quality and the international comparability of information that is vital both for the formulation of sound economic policies and for the smooth functioning of global financial markets," U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin said last week.
At the same time, officials are putting the final touches on a $54 billion war chest that can be used to help countries overwhelmed by economic crises similar to the Mexican debacle.

The pool of funds will be discussed during the annual meeting although final approval is unlikely at that time. It would double the amount in the General Arrangements to Borrow established by the Group of 10 industrial countries.

This doubling is to be accomplished by establishing a facility called the New Arrangements to Borrow with a number of countries, including Austria, Australia, Denmark, Finland, South Korea, Luxembourg, Malasia, Norway, Singapore, Spain and Thailand considering pledging funds to help in a crisis.

Policymakers will also discuss a new plan to assist poor countries hit by overwhelming debt, including outstanding loans to the IMF and World Bank. The plan could include the sale of some IMF gold but this has yet to be worked out.

But the debt relief plan has its critics. Officials attending this week's meeting of Commonwealth Finance Ministers in Bermuda take the view that the plan is so restrictive it will help few countries who really need it.

"These restrictions reduce to only 11 the number of countries likely to receive multilateral debt relief, and delay relief so that only three will receive comprehensive treatment," a confidential report at the meeting said.

Policymakers will also review proposals to increase the IMF's quota to help replenish the agency's coffers, hard hit by huge loans to Mexico and Russia in recent years. IMF Managing director Michel Camdessus is seeking a doubling to $440 billion.

Lastly, there will be discussion of a plan to allocate the IMF's own money, the Special Drawing Right, to newer members of the IMF that have been short-changed compared to older members. It is estimated this would amount to about 26 billion SDRS, or about $36 billion.
